chapter.title: Creating modular documentation

chapter.para: Modular documentation is an approach whose goal is to produce sets of adaptable, solution-based, easy-to-find and reusable documents from topics. Articles bundle these topics into assemblies. This chapter describes the topic types and explains how to write abstracts, add translation markup to assemblies and maintain revision histories.

Rather than covering a complete technology or a set of problems, each article serves one distinct purpose. Each article stands for itself, including requirements, context, instructions, troubleshooting and FAQs.
Modular documentation consists of topics—smaller information units that can be reused in different contexts. Four different topic types are available:

listitem.para: Task topics instruct the user how to perform certain tasks.
Concept topics explain underlying concepts to the users.
Reference topics inform the user about basic facts (settings, options, parameters, etc.).
Glue topics help navigate complex topics and provide links to related information.

chapter.para: Articles are built by bundling these topics into assembly files. An assembly file is an organizational that structures the topics into a coherent and meaningful document. For more information about the structure of an article, see .
To create a modular documentation project, use the templates for the assembly and its topical components. Find them in the doc-modular repository.

section.title: Creating optimized abstracts
section.para: An abstract helps both readers and search engines quickly understand the core value of the content. To align with modern search behaviors and optimize our documentation, write a solid introductory paragraph that acts as an AI-friendly answer nugget.
A good abstract provides a direct answer to the primary user intent. It should have the following structure:

listitem.para: Start with an objective, direct definition of the product or feature.
Explain the primary motivation and the technical advantage to the user.
State the benefits of the product or feature, where applicable.

section.para: If needed, add a clear list of requirements or prerequisites after the introductory paragraph. Do not use other lists, images or examples in an abstract. shows an abstract. shows an abstract with prerequisites.

example.title: Example of an abstract
example.para: SUSE Linux Enterprise Server can be deployed remotely over a network using the Preboot eXecution Environment (PXE) of the target device. By using PXE boot images provided by the network, administrators can efficiently provision fully operating and properly configured instances of SUSE Linux Enterprise Server. This approach needs no physical installation media.

example.title: Example of an abstract with prerequisites
example.para: SSH keys serve as an authentication method that allows access to an encrypted connection between systems. A key pair consists of a private key on the local machine and a public key on the remote server. Use SSH keys to automate logins without passwords and to enhance security against brute-force attacks.

listitem.para: An SSH client installed on the local machine
Permissions to modify the authorized keys on the remote server

section.title: Revision history
section.para: A revision history lists the high-level changes about the document itself. It gives readers an overview of important changes made over time. Search engines and large language models use the data as metadata and as a signal of content freshness.

Update the revision history regularly. Mention the most important changes when you amend or rework the document. The Revision History link appears before the abstract and opens a separate page. Keep in mind the following rules:

listitem.para: List revision entries in descending order by date. The latest entry must always come first.
Describe only significant changes that you performed.
Group several changes of the same type, such as additions, changes or removals, in an itemizedlist element.
Do not add links or references with xref of any kind. To mention a specific issue, use the abbreviations from the following page and wrap the issue in the uri element: .

section.para: To determine whether a change you made warrants a revision history entry, use this table:

table.title: Changes that warrant a revision history entry

row.entry: Added a new feature or deleted an obsolete one
Metadata fix, such as a new description or a change in the product name or version
Typo or grammar fixes, editorial reviews
